It also marks a new chapter for two brothers who have watched each other build careers, families and now, businesses. For Lola Beans founder Donny Bradley, the latest franchise deal is a little more personal than most. The growing drive-thru beverage brand has signed a six-unit franchise agreement to expand into Delaware with Donny’s brother, Jay Bradley, and his wife, Beth. The deal brings Lola Beans back to a place that already means something to the Bradley family. Donny and Jay grew up in Dover, Delaware, while their father was stationed at Dover Air Force Base, and Jay has continued to call Delaware home. Beth was born and raised in Delaware. Eight years ago, Jay & Beth moved 5 miles north, right over the line from the Delaware border to Southern Chester County, PA. Being a stone’s throw away from the DE/PA, we will always call Delaware home. It also marks a new chapter for two brothers who have watched each other build careers, families and now, businesses. Both found careers in the medical industry, with Donny previously working in medical device sales and Jay currently serving as a National Trainer for a spine biologics company. For Jay, bringing Lola Beans to Delaware is an opportunity to build something meaningful alongside his wife in a community they already know and love. Together, they plan to grow the concept throughout the state, bringing the same sense of connection, energy and community they have watched Donny and Missy build in Tennessee. “I’ve had a front-row seat to Lola Beans from the beginning, and I’ve watched Donny and Missy build something that is genuinely different,” said Jay Bradley. “It’s fun, it’s positive and it’s centered around making people’s day better. My wife and I are excited to bring that same energy to Delaware and build something our family can be proud of here.” “Watching Donny & Missy’s journey in Lola Beans inspired us….we have always wished we lived closer to them, so starting this new chapter gives us a little bit of our Chattanooga Family right here in Delaware/Pennsylvania.” “There’s something really special about your own family believing in what you’ve built enough to want to become part of it,” said Donny Bradley, co-founder of Lola Beans. “Jay has seen Lola Beans from the very beginning. He knows the hard work and everything that has gone into building it. For him and his family to say, ‘We want to bring this to Delaware,’ means a lot to Missy and me.” Donny’s career in medical device sales ultimately played an unexpected role in the Lola Beans story. In 2014, his work took him, Missy and their family to Soldotna, Alaska, where they became regulars at the area’s small drive-thru coffee huts. What stuck with them was the genuine connection and the way a quick interaction could turn around someone’s day. That experience eventually became the inspiration for Lola Beans. Donny and Missy opened the first Lola Beans in Chattanooga in 2020, followed by a second company-owned location in Cleveland, Tennessee. Today, they continue to invest in the concept themselves, with additional corporate growth planned in Tennessee alongside the brand’s franchise expansion. The Delaware agreement marks the latest step in that growth, bringing Lola Beans back to where the Bradley brothers’ story began while carrying the brand’s focus on good energy, genuine connection and community into a new state. articles.title: The Real Lesson in McDonald’s 515-Page Loyalty File
articles.titleKo: The Real Lesson in McDonald’s 515-Page Loyalty File
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . What unsettled the reporter wasn’t that McDonald’s had his data. It was seeing the backend terms laid bare. Last month, WIRED published an article from a reporter who requested his own McDonald’s loyalty data and was shocked when he got back 515 pages: every Monopoly prize he’d ever won, a predicted 2.16 visits over the next six weeks, an average order of $13.49, and a churn score of zero. He asked McDonald’s to delete his file and stopped eating there just to see if he could prove the algorithm wrong. The internet had a field day with just how much McDonald’s knew about the reporter. But if you run a restaurant with a loyalty program, chances are you are sitting on some version of this same data. The real question isn’t whether you have it. It’s whether you’re using it to make a guest feel actually known or just tracked. Guest data is a trade, not a form of surveillance Think of loyalty as a transaction, and data is the currency the guest spends. It’s the only currency a brand wants more than money, because it’s what makes better business decisions possible. That’s not a controversial take, even among the WIRED article’s readers. For example, several commenters shrugged at the McDonald’s report: tracking and forecasting purchases is a legitimate business case, and companies have been profiling regulars since the department store credit card. (One reader turned the question back on the outlet, asking whether WIRED could say what it stores on its own subscribers.) The reporter’s 515-page file is really a receipt for years of purchases. In exchange for reporting what he ate and when, he got perks and points that added up (and let’s not forget those Monopoly prizes). Both sides paid. Both sides collected. What unsettled the reporter wasn’t that McDonald’s had his data. It was seeing the backend terms laid bare, things like “attrition likelihood” and “RFM-derived top product.” Strip away the jargon, and 515 pages of transaction history built up over several years is a fairly ordinary amount of data. It’s what any brand needs to market effectively, forecast demand, and stay competitive in today’s environment. Creating personalized loyalty I worked in restaurants for 15 years before building software, and I lived the analog version of loyalty rewards. We’d walk regulars to their usual booths and have their favorite drinks waiting for them before they asked. In return, these guests gave us their feedback and their business. They didn’t feel watched. They felt known. Recreating that kind of personalized experience at scale used to require an entire team of analysts that only the biggest chains could afford. Most restaurant brands, even successful multi-unit ones, never had the resources to know a single guest that well, let alone act on it. Because of technology, that’s no longer true. A modern guest engagement platform builds one profile per guest across every ordering channel, then segments guests automatically by how recently, how often, and how much they’ve ordered. That segmentation is what turns “hasn’t ordered in 60 days” into an automatic win-back offer, or “always orders the same wrap” into a birthday reward that isn’t generic. Operators don’t need McDonald’s scale to do this anymore. They just need the right digital platform. A known guest who has offered their data should get something a stranger to the brand cannot buy: Order preferences that carry across channels, so they never have to re-enter them A pickup order that’s labeled with their name, thanking them for being a loyal guest First access to a limited item before it hits the full menu A comped item that shows up the day after a bad visit, unprompted, because the brand noticed Every one of these requires knowing the guest. As Dutch Bros and 7 Brew bid over sites, Black Rock Coffee Bar navigates publicly traded life , and Starbucks regains traction after years of choppiness , Scooter’s Coffee has steadily expanded in a category suddenly flush with growth brands. Scooter’s had 555 of its drive-thru-focused stores at the start of 2023. But that calendar proved a major catapult, with the company adding a net of 195 venues to exit at 650 (729 of which were franchised). Then, in 2024, Scooter’s grew by net 99 locations (96 franchised) and followed with development of 57 this past year, finishing at 906 (882 franchised and 24 affiliate run). It shouldn’t be long before the 1998-founded brand, which sprung up in Bellevue, Nebraska—the state’s oldest continuous settlement, dating back as a fur-trading post in the early 19 th Century—eclipses the 1,000-unit mark to join Dutch Bros (1,225 shops end of Q2), Starbucks (about 17,000 U.S.), and Dunkin’ ( roughly 10,000 ) as four-digit beverage brands. 7 Brew, at 800 or so today, is headed there, too, and should break through before the year turns over . Scooter’s likely will pass 1,000 sometime in 2027. According to its recent FDD, it’s planning 79 gross new franchised outlets across fiscal 2026 (and one company) and touts a pipeline of 242 agreements signed without a store opened yet. That includes 25 in Illinois, 22 in Florida, 20 in Texas, and double-digit deals inked in Georgia (11), Indiana (12), Michigan (11), Minnesota (15), and Missouri (11). This year’s growth webs out across a host of states, with a concentration of 12 planned for Illinois, seven in Indiana, and six apiece in Florida and Tennessee. That outline does not include potential closures. Scooter’s in 2025 opened 85 franchised restaurants, terminated two, had a non-renewal, and reacquired a location from a franchisee, Twenty-four Scooter’s ceased operations for “other reasons.” That number was 20 last year and two the year prior. Franchise openings have trended from 209 in 2023’s spurt (a year it sold 12 restaurants to franchisees) to 121 in 2024 and the noted 85 last calendar. Barring a material slide in trajectory, Scooter’s should be well within the 1,000-store orbit as 2027 comes into focus. As for how it compares by unit-level performance, Scooter’s finished 2025 with U.S. systemwide sales of $859 million and average-unit volumes just under $1 million. It marked the brand’s debut on the annual QSR 50 . CHECK OUT THE SNACK CATEGORY HERE Dutch Bros was at $2.2 billion systemwide sales and $2.1 million AUV, while 7 Brew reported $1.2 billion and $2.6 million, respectively. Starbucks was second only to McDonald’s overall in systemwide sales at $30.2 billion and generated AUVs hovering $1.8 million. Dunkin’ hit $13.1 billion and $1.4 million. Black Rock, which had 181 restaurants year-end (it recently crossed 200 ) achieved $200 million on AUVs of $1.3 million . Scooter’s unravels an extensive Item 19 on its FDD. The brand reports results for “kiosk drive-thru stores” and franchised “end-cap drive-thrus.” On average, the kiosk definition applies to a location 650–700 square feet, while end-caps are 800–1,400. And to note regarding the term “kiosk,” this is what Scooter’s uses to illustrate a drive-thru-only standalone box that’s not attached to other real estate. There is generally no seating and sales primarily owe to drinks and associated food products through drive-up windows. They are located in parking lots near other retail shopping. End-caps house in strip centers with indoor ordering and a drive-thru window. The “other” moniker comprises restaurants in hospitals, malls, schools, airports, sporting venues, free-standing buildings, and sometimes includes “substantial” indoor seating with a drive-thru and public restrooms, or stores with only a site-specific service counter. Grimaldi’s Pizzeria, the award-winning Brooklyn-style pizzeria known for its coal-fired, brick-oven pizza, today announced the sale of its Bell Tower Fort Myers location to UNIV Hospitality of Fort Myers, LLC, led by principals Gary Patel and Anil Harkhani. In connection with the acquisition, UNIV Hospitality has entered into a franchise development agreement with Grimaldi’s to open five additional restaurants across Sarasota, Lee and Collier counties, expanding the brand’s presence throughout Southwest Florida. Flaum, COO of Grimaldi’s Pizzeria. “Their experience and commitment to hospitality make them a strong partner as we continue to grow the Grimaldi’s brand.” “With the acquisition of Grimaldi’s Bell Tower restaurant and plans to expand across Southwest Florida, we look forward to building on the restaurant’s success and bringing Grimaldi’s to even more communities throughout the region,” said Anil Harkhani, UNIV Hospitality. “We plan to bring the same family-friendly, casual yet upscale atmosphere and award-winning pizzas to communities across southwest Florida.” Grimaldi’s is known for its coal-fired, brick-oven pizza and calzones, made with a secret recipe dough, sliced fresh mozzarella cheese and techniques dating back to more than 100 years in Brooklyn. Guests can also enjoy salads, starters and desserts, including Grimaldi’s famous house-made New York Style Cheesecake. The Bell Tower restaurant is located in Fort Myers, Florida, and will continue to operate under the Grimaldi’s Pizzeria brand as part of the UNIV Hospitality portfolio. Award-winning hospitality group Noble 33 announces Mr. Noble, an American brasserie concept built around upscale comfort food set to debut in Chicago’s River North neighborhood in early 2027. Located at 500 N. Clark St., the two-level restaurant will feature a lively restaurant upstairs and a subterranean speakeasy below, creating two distinct experiences under one roof. Mr. Noble is the second Chicago concept announced by Noble 33, following plans for a new Mexican-inspired concept slated for Fulton Market. Together, the two projects mark Noble 33’s entry into Chicago across two of the city’s most dynamic neighborhoods, each with its own distinct culinary point of view. “This is one of the most serious food cities in the country, and that’s exactly why we didn’t want to bring in something we’d already built somewhere else and just put a River North address on it,” said Noble 33 Co-Founder Tosh Berman. “Mr. Noble is a brand-new concept for Noble 33, and we’re excited for it to become Chicago’s own.” Mr. Noble will introduce a new category to Noble 33’s growing global portfolio, marking the hospitality group’s first concept centered around upscale American comfort food. The new brand joins Noble 33’s acclaimed collection, from Los Angeles to London, including Mēdüzā Mediterrania, Sparrow Italia, Toca Madera, Casa Madera and 1587 Prime. Upstairs at Mr. Noble, familiar dishes get steakhouse-level sourcing and technique, served with the ease of a neighborhood tavern. Downstairs, the mood shifts entirely as a dim, sultry speakeasy with live vocals gives guests a reason to make an entire evening out of their visit. The address itself has a storied place in River North’s dining history. Most recently, the space was home to Jaleo by chef José Andrés, which opened in 2021 and closed in January 2025, along with its basement speakeasy, Pigtail. Before that, the address was home to Michelin-starred restaurant Naha. “The moment we walked the space, we saw the potential,” said Noble 33 Co-Founder and CEO Mikey Tanha. “The building has character, history, and a two-level layout that let us build the framework for something we think River North is going to gather at for years to come.” The property is part of Friedman Properties’ longstanding River North portfolio. The family-run developer has played an integral role in the evolution of the neighborhood for more than five decades. “We’re excited to welcome Noble 33’s Mr. Noble to River North, further demonstrating the neighborhood’s staying power as Chicago’s most diverse and vibrant dining destination,” said Albert Friedman, chairman and CEO of Friedman Properties. “The addition of this national hospitality group complements the area’s established mix of dining, hospitality, office, residential and entertainment offerings and reflects its continued ability to attract new energy and investment.” For more information, visit noble33.com or follow @noble.33 on Instagram. The Flying Biscuit Café has signed a franchise agreement with franchisee Keisha Carter to bring the Atlanta-born all-day breakfast and brunch brand to McDonough, Ga., and the surrounding Henry County market. The site and opening date will be announced separately. Henry County is one of the fastest-growing counties in Georgia. Its population rose from 203,922 residents in 2010 to 240,712 in the 2020 census, and the U.S. Census Bureau estimated it at 264,922 in 2025. McDonough, the county seat and its largest city, sits along Interstate 75 about 30 miles southeast of downtown Atlanta. Carter, who lives in the market, said growth there has outpaced the area’s sit-down breakfast and brunch options — the gap that drew her to it. Carter brings nearly 10 years of experience in sales, business development, operations, client relations and team leadership, including roles at several Fortune 500 companies before moving into entrepreneurship. She holds an MBA in finance management and is a Six Sigma Black Belt, and currently leads a metro Atlanta real estate group where she oversees business operations, marketing, sales strategy, team development and client experience. She and her family have been Flying Biscuit regulars for years, and often talked about the south metro needing a location closer to home. Carter will partner with Eric Gladmon, who will serve as the venture’s main operating partner. Gladmon owns and operates an Atlanta salon that has been in business for more than 30 years, and brings that ownership and operations experience to the group. “Flying Biscuit has been an Atlanta staple and a longtime favorite for us as Georgia natives with deep roots in the area, so choosing a brand we already knew and loved felt natural,” said Keisha Carter, franchisee of the McDonough Flying Biscuit Café. “What makes this journey especially meaningful is that we get to do it as a family. After losing my mom in 2022, there’s something incredibly special about building this next chapter alongside my husband and my cousin, who shared such a close relationship with her. We’re excited to welcome the McDonough community into what we hope will feel like an extension of our own family.” The agreement covers one café, in McDonough. Carter has said she hopes to develop additional Flying Biscuit cafés in Georgia communities over time. She has also identified catering as a focus, pointing to Henry County’s school system, Piedmont Henry Hospital, local colleges, corporate offices, distribution centers and community organizations as potential customers. “Atlanta is where this brand started, and we’re still filling in pieces of the metro — Henry County is one of them,” said Andrew Scherzer, partner and director of franchise development for Flying Biscuit Franchising. “Keisha spent years wishing there were a Flying Biscuit closer to home, and now she’s the one bringing it. Operators who come to us as guests first tend to get the details right.” The McDonough café will serve The Flying Biscuit Café’s full breakfast and lunch menu, including its biscuits, shrimp and grits, omelets, vegan scrambles, burgers and wraps, along with full-service catering. The location, opening date and hiring details will be announced separately. More information about the brand is at flyingbiscuit.com. Prospective operators can find available markets, ownership requirements and how to start a conversation with the development team at flyingbiscuitfranchising.com. articles.title: The Case for Real Food: Why We Need the Salad More Than Ever
articles.titleKo: The Case for Real Food: Why We Need the Salad More Than Ever
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Real food doesn't need to reinvent itself to stay relevant. In recent weeks, the headlines have been heavy. Concerns regarding food safety have understandably caused many of us to pause, look at our plates and ask questions about where our food comes from and how it’s handled. These questions as not just necessary, but vital. When the world feels uncertain, I find myself returning to the basics. The most important decision any of us makes each day isn’t about our schedule or our to-do list — it’s the choice of how we fuel our bodies. Why Salads Still Matter We live in an era of ultra-processed convenience. While these options are fast, they often lack the foundational nutrients our bodies require to thrive. Consider that many grab-and-go meals are engineered for shelf life and speed, not for what they deliver nutritionally – a trade off most of us make without even realizing it. A well-constructed salad is the antithesis of this since it’s a powerhouse of nutrient density, delivering an unparalleled concentration of health-promoting compounds in every bite: Essential Micronutrients: Leafy greens and colorful vegetables carry vitamins A, C, and K, along with iron, folate, and potassium. These are the basics our immune systems and hearts actually depend on, and they’re the same nutrients most commonly missing from a fast-food value meal or a vending machine lunch. High-Impact Fiber : Fiber is the one nutrient most people underrate. It keeps digestion steady, blood sugar level, and it’s the reason a good salad keeps you full for hours instead of one. Most adults fall short of recommended daily fiber intake, and a single well-built salad can close a meaningful part of that gap in one sitting. Powerful Antioxidants: Antioxidants like lutein and beta-carotene fight the inflammation that builds up over time and support our eyes, our brains, our long-term health. These compounds don’t just protect against disease down the road, they are linked to sharper focus and steadier energy right now, which matters as much at 2 p.m. at your desk as it does decades from now. Bioavailability : Pair your greens with healthy fats like olive oil, avocado, or nuts, and you absorb more of those nutrients. It’s not just a salad at that point — it’s a system working the way it’s supposed to. That’s also why the format matters as much as the ingredients: a salad thrown together without any fat or protein leaves most of its potential on the table, while a thoughtfully composed one turns simple produce into something the body can actually use. Why the Salad is More Relevant Than Ever I still eat a salad most days. This isn’t because I have to, but because it’s one of the few decisions in our days that is entirely in our control. In a season full of headlines none of us can control, this matters more than it used to. This is why, despite the challenges facing our food system, the salad remains the gold standard. It’s a tool for personal control, allowing people to tailor their intake of lean proteins, healthy fats, and complex carbohydrates to meet their own goals — without ever sacrificing well-being for the sake of speed. Rebuilding Trust Through Transparency The recent wave of food safety headlines has shaken consumer confidence and some of that skepticism has been fair. Too often, “fresh” has been used as a marketing label instead of an operational standard. Rebuilding trust starts with transparency: knowing exactly where produce comes from, how it’s handled from farm to store and how many hands it passes through before it reaches a guest’s bowl. For us, this means shorter, more accountable supply chains; consistent, verifiable food-safety protocols across every location and a willingness to talk openly with guests about sourcing and handling, rather than treating it like a trade secret. In this environment, silence reads as evasion.

The 2026 cyclosporiasis outbreak has become the largest recorded in the United States. Two people in Michigan have died, more than 12,000 outbreak-linked cases have been reported in that state alone, and the outbreak has now spread across 15 states. Federal surveillance has lagged some state reporting, but the scale is clear: thousands of confirmed cases, thousands more under investigation, and growing concern among consumers. One major cluster has been traced to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms operations in central Mexico served at Taco Bell restaurants. Federal officials have linked 1,947 illnesses and at least 98 hospitalizations across nine states to that cluster. The consequences are no longer limited to public-health statistics. U.S. fresh-lettuce unit sales fell 9 percent during one week in July, and Taco Bell foot traffic was down more than 11 percent year over year on August 1 as the outbreak weighed on consumer confidence. For quick-service and fast-casual operators, the immediate issue is food safety. The larger operating question is why lettuce continues to be treated as a cheap, uncomplicated menu staple when its full cost includes refrigeration, spoilage, supply disruption, recall exposure, and brand risk. The restaurant industry has spent the past decade reconsidering nearly everything. Operators have rebuilt ordering systems, redesigned kitchens, introduced new labor models, expanded delivery, created loyalty platforms, adjusted portions, and rewritten menus around shifting costs. Lettuce has remained largely untouched. It is inexpensive, familiar, and expected on burgers, tacos, sandwiches, salads, and bowls. Those qualities have helped it avoid a more complicated question: Is lettuce still worth its full operating cost? Refrigeration Put Lettuce on the American Plate Iceberg lettuce rose alongside the modern American food-distribution system. Its compact, hardy head allowed growers to ship it farther than more delicate greens. California lettuce traveled across the country in ice-packed railcars beginning in the 1920s. The spread of refrigerated transportation, national grocery distribution, and household refrigeration made year-round lettuce increasingly practical. By 1950, iceberg was consumed more than any other vegetable in the United States. The cultivar fit the emerging system well. It was sturdy, standardized, mild, relatively inexpensive, and capable of surviving national transportation. That history explains how lettuce became embedded in American meals. It also illustrates how an operating choice can become a permanent assumption. Once an ingredient becomes broadly available, operators build purchasing contracts, equipment, recipes, portions, and customer expectations around its continued presence. Familiarity gradually begins to resemble necessity. The success of iceberg in the refrigerated supply chains of the twentieth century offers a historical explanation for its popularity. It does not settle whether every twenty-first-century menu still needs to be built around it. “We’ve always done it this way” remains a weak operating principle, even when the original decision made perfect sense. Chang’s in July 1993 in Scottsdale, Arizona. It’s grown to 20-plus countries and 300 global stores (about 200 in the U.S.) But it had begun to drift through ownership swaps and leadership moves. Mazany was named CEO in November 2025, making him the fourth lead executive in about two years. He succeeded former COO and CFO Brad Hill, who elevated in April and left after a few months. The transactions are a key piece of Red Robin’s First Choice Plan and its efforts to reduce debt and refinance its existing obligations. Red Robin has completed most of a sweeping refranchising initiative that shifted 108 restaurants to three multi-unit operators and brought the casual-dining chain roughly $89.4 million in proceeds. Eight additional locations are scheduled to close by the end of Red Robin’s 2026 fiscal year, pending the transfer of applicable liquor licenses. These restaurant sales are expected to bring in another $6.6 million, pushing the final tally to approximately $96 million. The transactions are a key piece of Red Robin’s First Choice Plan and its efforts to reduce debt and refinance its existing obligations. “Our talented team has made incredible progress in the execution of our First Choice Plan over the past year, and the completion of these refranchising agreements is a critical next step in strengthening our balance sheet as we position our business for sustainable, long-term growth,” CEO Dave Pace said in a statement. Op Burgers is purchasing the largest portion of the portfolio, with an agreement covering 69 restaurants across Kentucky, Indiana, Maryland, Ohio, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, and Virginia for $62.5 million. Kuber Oregon and Kuber Washington acquired 17 Red Robin restaurants in Oregon and Washington for $10 million. Evergreen Dining purchased another 30 locations in Washington and Western Idaho for $23.5 million. Red Robin first disclosed the Evergreen deal in May. The company said at the time that Evergreen’s principals had operated more than 100 restaurants across multiple national brands during nearly three decades in the industry. A few weeks later, Red Robin announced agreements with Op Burgers and Kuber. The chain has been working to improve its financial position and restaurant performance under Pace, who took over as CEO in 2025 and introduced the First Choice Plan. The strategy is built around protecting operational gains, driving traffic, cutting expenses and debt, investing in restaurant facilities and technology, and improving employee performance and retention. “Each of these seasoned operators shares our hospitality-first mindset and brings the resources needed to accelerate growth across these markets, while continuing to deliver an exceptional guest experience,” Pace said. “Importantly, these transactions will advance our efforts to refinance our existing debt and increase our financial flexibility.” Op Burgers said it plans to use its multi-unit operating experience to support employees across its newly acquired restaurants. Kuber pointed to Red Robin’s longstanding following in the Pacific Northwest, and Evergreen said it plans to help grow the brand across Washington and Idaho. Red Robin’s same-store sales rose 1.3 percent in the second quarter, with traffic down just 0.2 percent, the chain’s best traffic performance since early 2023. Traffic turned positive late in the quarter, and restaurant-level operating margin increased 20 basis points to 14.7 percent, its best Q2 result in four years. Red Robin has used value platforms such as Big Yummm, menu innovation, labor efficiencies, technology upgrades, and restaurant refreshes to support the turnaround. Salad and Go conducted an auction Monday between 7 Brew and Dutch Bros. The company entered the proceedings with 7 Brew as the lead bidder, and Dutch Bros ultimately elected not to submit a topping bid, according to bankruptcy court documents. Salad and Go subsequently named 7 Brew the successful bidder and Dutch Bros the backup bidder. The 73-site portfolio includes 41 locations in Arizona, 20 in Texas, and six each in Nevada and Oklahoma, according to court documents. 7 Brew is one of the fastest-growing concepts in America. It now has over 800 locations in 38 states. The company opened a net of 562 shops across 2023, 2024, and 2025. It earned $1.2 billion in sales last year and posted a $2.6 million AUV. READ MORE : Dutch Bros and 7 Brew to Battle for Salad and Go Locations Dutch Bros Strikes $105 Million Deal for Salad and Go Locations The outcome marks a significant turn from the transaction Salad and Go proposed when it filed for bankruptcy on August 4. Dutch Bros initially agreed to pay $105 million for 51 drive-thru restaurants in Arizona and Nevada, along with 14 leases in Texas and Oklahoma. But Salad and Go’s bankruptcy process left the door open for a higher offer. 7 Brew subsequently emerged as a competing bidder, setting up a head-to-head auction between two of the fastest-growing drive-thru beverage concepts in the country. Dutch Bros is entitled to a $3.8 million termination fee, plus reasonable and documented expenses, if the 7 Brew transaction closes. The final portfolio could still change before closing. 7 Brew can drop certain leases if it can’t operate its business at those locations. The sale comes after a dramatic retrenchment for Salad and Go. The brand, founded in Gilbert, Arizona, in 2013, had expanded to 146 restaurants at its peak before beginning a widespread closure program. Roughly 70 restaurants were slated for closure as the company pulled out of Texas and Oklahoma and concentrated its remaining operations in Arizona and Nevada. The restructuring also included the closure of its Garland, Texas, commissary. The contraction followed an aggressive period of development that left Salad and Go facing financial pressure. The company raised approximately $27 million in additional capital between December 2025 and January 2026 before ultimately filing for bankruptcy. 7 Brew’s winning bid gives the beverage chain access to dozens of existing drive-thru sites at a time when competition for suitable real estate has intensified across the industry. The transaction isn’t final. A court hearing is scheduled for September 21 to consider the transfer of the leases and contracts to 7 Brew. articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . For many years, franchising rewarded momentum. A compelling concept, solid unit growth, and a polished sales presentation were often enough to attract development interest. Not anymore. As inflation, higher labor costs, tighter lending standards, and shifting regulations reshaped the operating environment over the past year, prospective franchisees have become far more selective about where they invest. Excitement still matters, but it no longer closes the deal on its own. “The past year has really acted as a stress test, and not everyone passed,” says Liane Caruso, owner of helloCMO and cofounder of Franchise Assembly. “The brands that held up were the ones with lean, simple operations and realistic unit economics built for normal conditions.” That sentiment echoed across QSR’s 2026 Best Franchise Deals Council, a panel of franchise development, operations, marketing, legal, and investment experts assembled to help identify where the franchise industry is headed. The consensus was consistent. Franchise buyers are asking tougher questions than they were just a few years ago. They want proof instead of promises. They want to know how a concept performed when costs increased, labor tightened, and financing became more difficult—not simply how it grew during years of favorable market conditions. “A franchise that looks attractive on paper is selling a story. A strong franchise opportunity is selling proof,” says Michelle Rowan, president of Franchise Business Review. Today’s buyers, she says, are looking past projections to unit-level profitability, franchisee satisfaction, and candid validation from existing operators. Jonathan Hill, cofounder of Morrow Hill, has watched the same shift unfold from the real estate side. Inflation and labor pressures have forced brands to simplify operations, improve efficiency, and demonstrate predictable financial performance. “Clear, conservative financials and predictable cash flow are becoming table stakes,” he says. John Francis, whose franchise career spans more than three decades as a franchisee, franchisor, investor, and board member, believes prospective operators are also evaluating the strength of the organization behind the concept. “Paper looks the same for almost every brand,” he says. “What separates the real opportunities is operational discipline behind the curtain.” He argues the strongest systems have evolved beyond founder-led businesses into organizations with the infrastructure, leadership, and processes necessary to support long-term expansion. Those changing expectations explain why some brands continue signing development agreements while others struggle to fill their pipelines. Council members repeatedly pointed to the same characteristics. Winning franchise systems demonstrate durable unit economics instead of relying on exceptional performers. They simplify operations, embrace technology that improves productivity, offer flexible development options, and provide meaningful support long after opening day. These successful chains are also attracting experienced multi-unit operators who are evaluating whether the underlying business is built to scale. This year’s Best Franchise Deals list represents more than high-performing brands. They showcase franchise systems that have earned confidence through transparency, operational discipline, and a proven ability to help franchisees succeed in a more demanding business environment. articles.title: The Rise of the Anti-Brand Bakery
articles.titleKo: The Rise of the Anti-Brand Bakery
articles.originalSummary: “Long live non-conformity,” says Cornish Bakery Founder Steve Grocutt as he debuts new RISE concept Fast growing Cornish Bakery is breaking the normal rules of expansion, turning its back on cookie-cutter brand building. The company has gone through three successful brand identities and is now starting afresh again. Founder Steve Grocutt says, “We’ve built a successful bakery brand with 81 locations and now we’re tearing it all apart. All on purpose. Five years ago, we took the DBA Gold award-winning Cornish Bakery brand we had honed at the time, and we completely ditched it! A lot of people thought we were mad, but I instinctively knew we had to move on. There was an urgency not to fall into a homogenous brand building category.” At the time, it was Grocutt’s mantra that led this direction. His simple, pioneering, guiding mantra: ‘bakery is the new coffee shop’ set the route. Five years on, Cornish Bakery’s growth has more than proven that statement to be spot on. The company has doubled its number of bakeries, grown the team to over 1,000, quadrupled profit and has developed enviable customer NPS scores of 75%. Steve continues, “We led with our vision to nourish people and reset the bakery design compass, all whilst delivering on our stated mission to redefine what a bakery is, does, and can be.” The team identified a handful of larger sites, spaces “crying out for that added extra” thus ‘RISE by Cornish Bakery’ was born, a bigger, bolder licensed brand extension. Sites in Betws-y-Coed, Wales, and Gunwharf Quays, Portsmouth, are now open and, in Grocutt’s words are, “already hammering it out of the park in every way possible.” “With RISE by Cornish Bakery we’ve reshaped what a bakery is does and can be. We’re thinning the boundary between bakeries/coffee shops and casual dining spaces, extending trading hours and integrating more deeply into the social fabric, the ‘vibe’, and the wishes and needs of the surrounding community – all led and driven by our brilliant colleagues on the ground.” The first RISE opened two months ago in Betws-y-Coed, Wales. The second is at Portsmouth’s historic Gunwharf Quays Designer Outlet where Cornish Bakery has relocated into a new two-storey, 3,500 sq. ft property as part of the centre’s redevelopment, making it the company’s largest site to date. RISE by Cornish Bakery Gunwharf Quays features an orangery, an outdoor terrace, a first-floor balcony, and dedicated space for community baking and barista classes. By high school, Calvo was put into a cooking class by mistake. She calls this the “lightning strike” of her career. “While I was waiting to get my schedule fixed, Johnson & Wales University came in and did a demo of this beautiful stuffed brioche French toast, and it was like I felt myself being put on the right path,” Calvo says. “I went home that day and told my parents, ‘I’m going to be a chef.'” In culinary school, Calvo began entering culinary competitions to help pay off her student debt. She would go on to become one of the nation’s youngest cookbook authors. “The judge told me, ‘You’re winning based on one thing, and that’s flavor. When you put those recipes together, call that cookbook “Maximum Flavor.”‘ That stayed in the back of my mind,” Calvo says. “Before I know it, I’m in New York City with my family on ‘The Montel Williams Show.'” Despite her early career success, her personal life was upended. Calvo’s younger sister, Jennifer, passed suddenly from a rare form of cancer. Heartbroken, Calvo stopped cooking. Then she saw an ad for an affordable restaurant space in Miami. She felt lightning strike again, like a push from above. She maxed out her credit cards and took the money from her cookbook sales to open Chef Adrianne’s Vineyard Restaurant and Bar at the age of 22. “I had no business experience, just a belief in making really great food and loving to serve people the way my mom served us growing up, with genuine hospitality,” Calvo says. “We opened in an unassuming shopping center, and here we are, 20 years later.” She has watched Miami’s culinary landscape evolve over the years, from the traditional Cuban bakeries she visited as a teenager to the wider array of Colombian, Venezuelan and Caribbean influences that have emerged alongside the city’s growing Latino communities. “The younger generations are culture hungry. As an 8MW wind farm, it generates approximately 17 gigawatt-hours of renewable energy annually. One of the most innovative aspects is the real-time, half-hourly matching of BKUK’s electricity use with the wind farm’s output, enabling non-standard cost savings while helping to reduce emissions. We’re proud to support BKUK integrate more renewable energy into its operations.” Evolve Energy and Alaska Wind Farm LLP were introduced by Sustainable Energy First (SE First), BKUK’s trusted advisory partner commissioned to source a long-term renewable energy solution aligned with BKUK’s energy requirements and sustainability commitments. To help BKUK reduce its reliance on non-renewable energy, SE First partnered with Evolve Energy for its ability to secure direct access to a generator and supply their energy through a CPPA. articles.title: Pimentae Expands Beyond Tequiloa with the Launch of it’s First Ever Spicy Mezcal Margartita
articles.titleKo: Pimentae Expands Beyond Tequiloa with the Launch of it’s First Ever Spicy Mezcal Margartita
articles.originalSummary: Award-winning tequila cocktail brand Pimentae is stepping into an exciting new chapter with the launch of its first-ever Spicy Mezcal Margarita – the brand’s first move beyond tequila and into the captivating world of mezcal. For founders Alice Parmiter and Wynter Karo, the launch is a natural evolution of Pimentae’s love affair with agave spirits. As more consumers discover the rich complexity behind mezcal, the category is becoming one of the most exciting new areas of exploration within premium drinks. Launching in selected Waitrose and Co-op stores from the June, the new ready-to-drink cocktail has been created in partnership with acclaimed Mexican producer Ojo de Dios Mezcal, bringing a distinctive new flavour profile to the growing RTD category. Combining smoky mezcal, fresh lime, sweet agave and a gentle jalapeño kick, the Spicy Mezcal Margarita offers a deeper, more intriguing take on Pimentae’s signature style. Bold yet balanced, it is designed for curious drinkers looking to discover something new. A cocktail that invites you to slow down, savour the moment and explore the smoky, complex character that makes mezcal so special. The launch represents a natural evolution for the female-founded brand, which has built its reputation as one of the UK’s leading tequila cocktail specialists. “Tapping into mezcal is a natural next step for us and opens the door to a slightly different consumer and occasion, “ says Alice Parmiter, co founder of Pimentae. “ A lot of people don’t actually realise that tequila is a type of mezcal. Where tequila is often bright, crisp and citrus-led, mezcal has a deeper, smokier and more complex profile that tends to appeal to those who might gravitate towards whisky or darker spirits. As consumers become more educated and curious about agave, mezcal has become a real point of discovery. It still feels niche enough to be exciting, but culturally it’s building huge momentum.” Wynter Karo says: “We never built Pimentae to simply repeat what already exists in the category. Mezcal gave us the opportunity to bring genuine newness into the RTD space. “ Inspired by mezcal’s deep cultural roots and the landscapes of Mexico, the Spicy Mezcal Margarita celebrates mezcal’s mystical origins, ancestral craftsmanship and enduring connection to the land. The serve balances smoke, citrus and spice to create what Pimentae describes as a “dance of fire and earth, smoke and citrus”. Rich notes of mezcal are lifted by fresh lime and agave sweetness, while a gentle chilli warmth lingers on the finish. The launch of Spicy Mezcal Margarita signals the next phase of Pimentae’s ambition to lead the premium agave cocktail category, bringing consumers new ways to explore the complexity, culture and craftsmanship behind Mexico’s most celebrated spirits.

articles.originalSummary: Para celebrar dez anos como patrocinadora oficial da Conmebol Libertadores, a Amstel, cerveja puro malte do Grupo Heineken , lançou no Brasil uma edição especial de suas latas inspirada no troféu do campeonato, disponível nos formatos de 269 ml, 350 ml e 473 ml, além do six-pack de long necks. A edição foi desenvolvida para marcar a 67ª edição da competição, e a Amstel espera ampliar sua distribuição, com crescimento de volume de três dígitos e presença em todas as regiões do Brasil, especialmente no Sul, Sudeste e Nordeste. Nos demais países que sediam partidas da Conmebol Libertadores, a marca também lançará campanhas e ações locais ao longo do torneio, voltadas aos torcedores. “O futebol sul-americano sempre foi uma das formas de a Amstel se conectar com as pessoas e, junto com iniciativas de música e diversidade, reflete nossa crença de que as marcas mais fortes são construídas a partir da criação de espaços onde todos possam se encontrar”, comenta Cecilia Bottai, vice-presidente de Marketing do Grupo Heineken. A iniciativa marca o retorno do torneio após a Copa do Mundo Fifa e o início de uma nova fase de ações da marca para a competição, que serão realizadas ao longo do torneio. Presença nos supermercados A Amstel também está ampliando sua presença nos pontos de venda com um móvel temático criado para reunir, em um único espaço do supermercado, os principais itens utilizados em churrascos e facilitar a jornada de compra. Batizado de Churrasco Amstel, o equipamento foi desenvolvido em parceria com a agência Tiwa Creative e está disponível em lojas de diferentes regiões do Brasil. A solução foi desenvolvida para supermercados e tem como proposta oferecer conveniência ao consumidor ao centralizar tudo o que é necessário para organizar o churrasco em um único espaço. Posicionado próximo ao açougue, o móvel reúne cervejas Amstel, carvão, molhos, temperos, espetos e outros itens utilizados em churrascos. Entre os recursos do móvel está a calculadora de churrasco Amstel, apresentada em uma tela interativa. Ao informar o número de convidados e a duração do evento, o sistema indica a quantidade estimada de cerveja Amstel, além de refrigerante, água, cortes de carne e acompanhamentos. articles.originalSummary: Motoristas que pretendem adesivar veículos com propaganda eleitoral ou utilizá-los em atividades de campanha nas eleições 2026 devem informar previamente a seguradora para evitar problemas em caso de sinistro. O alerta é da Federação Nacional de Seguros Gerais (FenSeg). Segundo Keila Farias, vice-presidente da Comissão de Seguro Auto da entidade, a adesivação pode ser vista pelas seguradoras como um fator de aumento de risco, devido à maior exposição do veículo a acidentes, vandalismo e eventos públicos. A FenSeg acrescenta que mudanças no perfil de uso do veículo sem atualização da apólice podem resultar em recusa de indenização por roubo, furto ou colisão. As seguradoras argumentam que a utilização do carro para transporte de material de campanha, deslocamento de equipes ou atividades de apoio altera as condições avaliadas quando o contrato foi firmado. A entidade também destaca que danos a adesivos, plotagens e envelopamentos geralmente não estão cobertos pelos seguros convencionais. Além disso, prejuízos decorrentes de tumultos, motins e atos de vandalismo costumam estar entre as exclusões previstas nos contratos. Como evitar a perda da cobertura: Informar a seguradora antes de adesivar o veículo; Comunicar qualquer mudança na utilização do carro durante a campanha eleitoral; Consultar o corretor de seguros antes de prestar serviços a candidatos ou partidos; Solicitar um endosso para registrar formalmente a alteração na apólice, quando necessário; Verificar se o envelopamento exige atualização do registro do veículo junto ao Detran; Conferir quais danos e situações estão excluídos da cobertura contratada; Com informações de Agência Brasil. articles.title: INPC registra deflação em julho e acumula alta de 4,10% em 12 meses
articles.titleKo: INPC registra deflação em julho e acumula alta de 4,10% em 12 meses
articles.originalSummary: O Índice Nacional de Preços ao Consumidor (INPC), utilizado para a correção anual de salários, fechou julho com deflação de 0,01%. No acumulado de 12 meses, o indicador está em 4,1%. Os dados foram divulgados nesta terça-feira, 11, pelo Instituto Brasileiro de Geografia e Estatística ( IBGE ). A última vez em que o INPC registrou deflação foi em agosto de 2025 (-0,21%). No ano de 2026, o índice acumula alta de 3,5%. O IBGE informou também que o Índice Nacional de Preços ao Consumidor Amplo (IPCA), conhecido como inflação oficial, fechou julho em 0,07% e soma 4,44% em 12 meses, puxado pelo recuo no custo dos alimentos. INPC X IPCA A diferença entre os dois índices é que o INPC apura a variação de preços para famílias com renda de um até cinco salários mínimos. Já o IPCA, afere a variação para lares com renda de um até 40 salários mínimos. Atualmente o valor do salário mínimo é de R$ 1.621. No INPC são apurados preços de 367 produtos e serviços (os chamados subitens), dez a menos que no IPCA. O IBGE confere pesos diferentes aos grupos de preços pesquisados. No INPC, por exemplo, os alimentos representam cerca de 25% do índice, mais que no IPCA (aproximadamente 21%), pois as famílias de menor renda gastam proporcionalmente mais com comida. Na ótica inversa, o preço de passagem de avião pesa menos no INPC do que no IPCA. Cálculo salarial O INPC influencia diretamente a vida de muitos brasileiros pois o acumulado móvel de 12 meses costuma ser utilizado para o cálculo do reajuste de salários de diversas categorias ao longo do ano. O salário mínimo, por exemplo, leva o dado de novembro no seu cálculo. O seguro-desemprego, o teto do INSS e o benefício de quem recebe acima do salário mínimo são reajustados com base no resultado do INPC acumulado até dezembro. De acordo com o IBGE, a apuração do INPC “tem por objetivo a correção do poder de compra dos salários, através da mensuração das variações de preços da cesta de consumo da população assalariada com mais baixo rendimento”. A coleta de preços do INPC é feita em dez regiões metropolitanas: Belém, Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador, Belo Horizonte, Vitória, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Curitiba e Porto Alegre. A coleta também é feita em Brasília, Goiânia, Campo Grande, Rio Branco, São Luís e Aracaju. Com informações de Agência Brasil. articles.title: BC aponta desaceleração da inflação, mas mantém alerta sobre riscos
articles.titleKo: BC aponta desaceleração da inflação, mas mantém alerta sobre riscos
articles.originalSummary: A ata da reunião em que o Comitê de Política Monetária (Copom) reduziu a taxa básica de juros (Selic) para 14% ao ano mostra que a decisão foi tomada em um ambiente de desaceleração da inflação , mas ainda marcado por incertezas. As expectativas inflacionárias, segundo o documento divulgado pelo Banco Central nesta terça-feira, 11, permanecem elevadas em um cenário de riscos. O comitê avalia que a redução da taxa Selic é “compatível com a estratégia de convergência da inflação para o redor da meta”. Na avaliação, a instituição ressalta ainda que, além de contribuir para a estabilidade de preços, a decisão ajuda a atenuar oscilações da atividade econômica e favorece o pleno emprego. Apesar do corte dos juros, o comitê afirma que o cenário exige prudência. A ata conclui que a política monetária vem contribuindo de forma importante para o processo de desinflação, mas destaca que a inflação continua pressionada pela demanda. Por isso, o Banco Central entende que os juros ainda precisam permanecer em nível restritivo. Projeções No cenário de referência usado pelo Banco Central, a trajetória dos juros considera as projeções do Boletim Focus. Já a taxa de câmbio parte de R$ 5,10 por dólar e evolui de acordo com a paridade do poder de compra. Inflação e política fiscal O documento registra que a inflação ao consumidor desacelerou nas leituras mais recentes, mas continua acima do limite superior da meta. Já os preços ao produtor apresentaram recuo, influenciados principalmente pelo comportamento da indústria extrativa, responsável pela obtenção de recursos naturais, como minérios, petróleo, gás natural e carvão. Os diretores alertam que o crescimento do crédito direcionado e as incertezas em relação à estabilização da dívida pública têm potencial para pressionar as taxas de juros da economia. Cenário externo Com relação ao cenário internacional, a ata avalia que as incertezas permanecem elevadas. Entre os fatores de preocupação estão os desdobramentos dos conflitos no Oriente Médio e as dúvidas em relação à condução da política monetária em economias avançadas. O comitê vê um ambiente marcado pela volatilidade nos preços de ativos financeiros e commodities, exigindo cautela por parte dos países emergentes. O documento chama a atenção para as incertezas em torno da política econômica dos Estados Unidos, fator que, segundo a ata, continua contribuindo para o cenário internacional instável. Cenário interno O Copom observa sinais de moderação gradual da atividade econômica interna desde a última reunião. Segundo o comitê, a economia manteve trajetória de desaceleração. Ainda que com perda de ritmo, o mercado de trabalho continua aquecido, e a taxa de desemprego permanece em níveis historicamente baixos, embora o crescimento da ocupação esteja desacelerando. Os rendimentos médios dos trabalhadores perderam força, mas “ainda crescem em termos reais a uma taxa superior à da produtividade do trabalho”, avalia o Copom. Com informações de Agência Brasil. As expectativas inflacionárias, segundo o documento divulgado pelo Banco Central nesta terça-feira, 11, permanecem elevadas em um cenário de riscos.

articles.title: 29 setores conhecerão Plano de Apoio da ApexBrasil a prejudicados pelo tarifaço de Trump
articles.titleKo: 29 setores conhecerão Plano de Apoio da ApexBrasil a prejudicados pelo tarifaço de Trump
articles.originalSummary: Representantes de 29 setores produtivos brasileiros afetados pelas tarifas impostas pelo governo dos Estados Unidos do presidente norte-americano, Donald Trump, estão reunidos com o ministro do Desenvolvimento, Indústria, Comércio e Serviços, Márcio Elias Rosa, em São Paulo, no ambiente do Plano de Diversificação de Exportações. O plano está sendo apresentado pela Agência Brasileira de Promoção de Exportações e Investimentos ( ApexBrasil ), no WTC Events Center e é voltado justamente para apoiar as empresas prejudicadas pelo tarifaço. O número de setores participantes do evento foi passado ao Broadcast pelo próprio ministro Elias Rosa numa troca rápida de palavras com a reportagem. O próprio ministro toma conhecimento agora do plano de apoio elaborado pela ApexBrasil, apresentado pelo presidente da agência, Laudemir Müller, e pela diretora de Negócios, Maria Paula Velloso. “Além das empresas que já fazem parte da base de atendimento da ApexBrasil, a agência estruturou novas ações e estratégias de inteligência comercial para atender ao universo de 5.400 empresas brasileiras estimadas como atingidas pelo tarifaço, com o objetivo de mitigar perdas e redirecionar os esforços de exportação para novos mercados”, diz o material de apoio confeccionado pela ApexBrasil. Tarifa dos EUA afeta 18% das exportações brasileiras Márcio Elias Rosa, afirmou que a nova tarifa anunciada pelos Estados Unidos deverá atingir cerca de 18% das exportações brasileiras destinadas ao mercado norte-americano, o equivalente a US$ 7,4 bilhões, considerando os embarques registrados em 2024. Segundo ele, se considerada a pauta exportadora de 2025, a participação dos setores alcançados pela medida cai para 15% das vendas aos Estados Unidos, correspondendo a US$ 5,8 bilhões. “Nós vamos ter cerca de 18% das nossas exportações para os EUA atingidas, o que corresponde a US$ 7,4 bilhões de dólares. Isso levando em conta o ano de 2024, antes, portanto, do início do tarifaço. Se considerarmos 2025, a participação desses setores atingidos por esse tarifaço indevido, 4,8% ou US$ 5,8 bilhões”, disse, durante entrevista coletiva. Com informação do Estadão de Conteúdo (Francisco Carlos de Assis). articles.title: TSMC e Sony anunciam investimento de US$ 4,7 bi em joint venture para sensores de imagem
articles.titleKo: TSMC e Sony anunciam investimento de US$ 4,7 bi em joint venture para sensores de imagem
articles.originalSummary: A fabricante taiwanesa de chips TSMC e a Sony anunciaram nesta terça-feira, 11, uma joint venture de US$ 4,69 bilhões para desenvolver e fabricar sensores de imagem de última geração para smartphones . A nova empresa funcionará no sul do Japão, com produção em escala prevista para começar em 2029 com tecnologia de processo avançada. Pelo acordo, a Sony planeja contribuir com cerca de 465 bilhões de ienes (US$ 2,92 bilhões), por meio de uma combinação de aportes em dinheiro e transferência de ativos. A TSMC, por sua vez, pretende aportar aproximadamente 282 bilhões de ienes (US$ 1,77 bilhão) em dinheiro. As contribuições devem ser feitas em fases, conforme a demanda do mercado e outras condições comerciais. O estabelecimento da joint venture e a conclusão da transação dependem de aprovações regulatórias e do cumprimento de outras condições habituais de fechamento, acrescentaram as empresas. Crescimento das vendas Em paralelo, a TSMC divulgou um crescimento na receita de julho acima das estimativas, reforçando que a demanda por Inteligência Artificial (IA) continua em forte expansão. A receita de julho da companhia foi de 467,58 bilhões de novos dólares taiwaneses (US$ 14,50 bilhões), aumento de 45% em relação ao mesmo mês do ano anterior. Em seus resultados mais recentes, a TSMC elevou sua previsão de crescimento de receita para 2026 para mais de 40% em termos de dólares americanos, de 30% anteriormente. Embora a TSMC não divulgue comentários ou uma análise detalhada de sua receita junto com os números mensais, seu crescimento está sendo impulsionado pela necessidade de chips de IA. Para o período de janeiro a julho, suas vendas ano a ano aumentaram 37%. A TSMC é o principal fornecedor de chips para a Nvidia , líder em semicondutores usados para aplicações de IA. A TSMC também fabrica os processadores principais dentro dos iPhones da Apple, chipsets móveis da Qualcomm e processadores fabricados pela Advanced Micro Devices (AMD). Com informação do Estadão de Conteúdo (Thais Porsch). articles.titleKo: Itaúsa tem lucro líquido recorrente de R$ 4,3 bilhões no 2T, alta de 7%
articles.originalSummary: A Itaúsa, holding de investimentos que integra o bloco de controle do Itaú Unibanco, registrou lucro líquido recorrente de R$ 4,3 bilhões no segundo trimestre de 2026, alta de 7% em relação a igual intervalo de 2025, de acordo com balanço divulgado nesta segunda-feira, 10. No primeiro semestre, o ganho foi de R$ 8,8 bilhões, avanço anual de 12%. O principal motor do resultado foi o desempenho do Itaú Unibanco, cuja contribuição para a holding somou R$ 4,468 bilhões entre abril e junho, crescimento de 8,5% em base anual. Entre os investimentos não financeiros, a Alpargatas contribuiu com R$ 55 milhões, incremento de 85,7% em um ano. A Motiva gerou R$ 69 milhões, alta de 66,9%, enquanto a Copa Energia entregou R$ 102 milhões, expansão de 17,3%. A participação da Dexco foi de R$ 2 milhões, queda de 74% na comparação anual. Na contramão, Aegea Saneamento apresentou resultado negativo de R$ 14 milhões, que representa uma elevação anual de 34,2%. Já a NTS deu um saldo negativo de R$ 68 milhões, revertendo o positivo de R$ 45 milhões em igual período de 2025. No total, o portfólio de empresas não financeiras gerou resultado recorrente de R$ 141 milhões para a Itaúsa no trimestre em junho, recuo de 26,7% ante um ano. Já as despesas administrativas da holding somaram R$ 45 milhões no segundo trimestre, aumento de 7% em base anual. No relatório que acompanha o balanço, o presidente da companhia, Alfredo Setubal, afirma que, apesar da gradual redução da Selic, o ambiente ainda é caracterizado por condições financeiras “restritivas, cautela de agentes econômicos e incerteza internacional”. “Mesmo diante desse contexto, seguimos executando nossa estratégia de geração sustentável de valor, apoiados pela disciplina na alocação de capital e pela gestão ativa do nosso portfólio”, ressaltou. Ainda conforme o executivo, os números da Dexco foram pressionados pelo segmento de celulose solúvel, diante da queda no preço, além de desafios setoriais em revestimentos cerâmicos. Já a Aegea foi afetada pela piora no resultado financeiro. “Os resultados do investimento na NTS foram impactados, em relação ao ano anterior, pela variação negativa no valor justo do ativo”, acrescentou. articles.originalSummary: A Caixa Seguridade registrou lucro líquido gerencial de R$ 1,14 bilhão no segundo trimestre de 2026, alta de 9,5% em relação a igual intervalo de 2025. Na comparação com o primeiro trimestre de 2026, houve queda de 0,2%, de acordo com a companhia . As receitas operacionais subiram 8,5% em um ano, para R$ 1,5 bilhão. As empresas em que a holding tem participação responderam por R$ 884,7 milhões das receitas, avanço de 11% no confronto anual. As receitas com comissionamento subiram 5,2% na mesma base comparativa, para R$ 615,3 milhões. A margem operacional subiu 5,5 pontos percentuais na comparação anual e 9,0 pontos percentuais no semestre, impulsionada pelo avanço dos prêmios ganhos em seguros de pagamento mensal. Em relação ao primeiro trimestre do ano, o indicador refletiu o aumento nas despesas operacionais e no volume de sinistros. O Retorno sobre o Patrimônio Líquido (ROE) recorrente atingiu 70,9% no segundo trimestre, uma alta de 1,3 ponto percentual na comparação anual. Na relação com o primeiro trimestre, o avanço foi de 5,0 pontos percentuais, impulsionado pelo ganho no lucro acumulado de 12 meses e pela gestão do patrimônio líquido e dividendos. O resultado financeiro foi de R$ 45,1 milhões no segundo trimestre, queda de 0,8% em relação a igual período de 2025. Por outro lado, o resultado operacional aumentou 9,5%, a R$ 1,23 bilhão. Ciberataques geram R$ 20 mi em prejuízos O presidente da Caixa Econômica Federal, Carlos Vieira, disse que o banco teve cerca de R$ 20 milhões de prejuízos na aplicativo Caixa Tem em 2025 por fraudes relacionadas a ataques cibernéticos . Por isso, o banco público vem reforçando investimentos em tecnologia. Para 2026, esses investimentos devem somar R$ 5,9 bilhões. Vieira disse que o banco tem um crescimento em implantações tecnológicas de 22,5%. “Nós estamos agora com praticamente zero de ataques no Caixa Tem”, disse Vieira em entrevista à imprensa. O banco teve 3,4 milhões de contas digitais abertas, sendo 1,6 milhão abertas no primeiro trimestre de 2026, destacou o presidente do banco – 49% dessas contas foram abertas pela geração Z. articles.titleKo: Inflação desacelera para 0,07% em julho puxada por alimentos
articles.originalSummary: A inflação, medida pelo IBGE , perdeu força pelo quarto mês seguido e fechou em 0,07% em julho ante 0,16% em junho. No acumulado de 12 meses, o IPCA está em 4,44%, abaixo do centro da meta estabelecida pelo Banco Central (4,5%). Os dados indicam que os alimentos caíram de preço e puxaram a inflação para baixo. O IPCA de julho veio em linha com a estimativa do mercado financeiro. O boletim Focus desta segunda-feira (10), sondagem do Banco Central (BC) com instituições econômicas, projetava que a inflação de julho ficaria em 0,07%. Para o fim de 2026, o mercado espera IPCA em 5,02%. Dentro da meta O comportamento dos preços fez com que o acumulado de 12 meses (4,44%) entrasse novamente na meta do governo: de 3%, com tolerância de 1,5 ponto percentual para mais ou para menos, ou seja, um intervalo de 1,5% a 4,5%. Em abril, o acumulado estava em 4,39%, mas o índice extrapolou o limite máximo em maio (4,72%) e junho (4,64%). Desde o início de 2025, o período de avaliação da meta é referente aos 12 meses imediatamente passados e não apenas ao alcançado no fim do ano (dezembro). A meta é considerada descumprida se a inflação estourar o intervalo de tolerância por seis meses seguidos. Julho O resultado de julho foi o menor desde agosto de 2025, quando o IPCA marcou 0,11%. Levando em consideração apenas os meses de julho, o desempenho do mês passado é o menor desde 2022 (-0,68). O índice de difusão em julho, que mostra o quanto a inflação está espalhada no mês, foi de 50%, ou seja, metade dos 377 produtos e serviços pesquisados pelo IBGE tiveram aumento de preço. Confira como foi o comportamento dos preços e o impacto em ponto percentual (p.p.) nos nove grupos pesquisados pelo IBGE: Alimentação e bebidas: -0,67% (-0,14 p.p.) Habitação: 0,99% (0,15 p.p.) Educação: -0,03% (0 p.p.) Comunicação: 0,04% (0 p.p.) O índice O IPCA apura o custo de vida para famílias com rendimentos entre um e 40 salários mínimos. Ao todos, são coletados preços de 377 subitens (produtos e serviços). A coleta de preços é feita em dez regiões metropolitanas – Belém, Fortaleza, Recife, Salvador, Belo Horizonte, Vitória, Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Curitiba, Porto Alegre – além de Brasília e nas capitais Goiânia, Campo Grande, Rio Branco, São Luís e Aracaju. articles.title: BTG Pactual tem lucro líquido ajustado de R$ 5,1 bilhões no 2º trimestre
articles.titleKo: BTG Pactual tem lucro líquido ajustado de R$ 5,1 bilhões no 2º trimestre
articles.originalSummary: O BTG Pactual encerrou o segundo trimestre com lucro líquido ajustado de R$ 5,1 bilhões, um aumento de 23% em 12 meses. As receitas totais do banco somaram R$ 10,4 bilhões, uma alta de 16% em 12 meses. O retorno sobre o patrimônio ajustado (ROAE) encerrou o período em 26,7%, abaixo dos 27,2% do mesmo intervalo de 2025 e levemente acima dos 26,6% do primeiro trimestre. A entrada líquida de recursos recuou para R$ 59 bilhões no segundo trimestre, em comparação ao primeiro trimestre, quando alcançou R$ 82,8 bilhões. O banco informou que o total de ativos sob custódia na Asset e no segmento Wealth cresceu 25% em 12 meses, para R$ 2,7 trilhões. Os ativos totais do BTG Pactual somaram R$ 925,2 bilhões no segundo trimestre, um aumento de 9,4% em comparação com o primeiro trimestre . O índice de Basileia fechou o trimestre em 16%, contra 16,2% no segundo trimestre de 2025. O patrimônio foi para R$ 79,6 bilhões no segundo trimestre de 2026, acima dos R$ 63,7 bilhões no mesmo intervalo de 2025. “Entregamos mais um trimestre de resultados recordes, refletindo a solidez e a diversificação da nossa plataforma, bem como nossa capacidade de capturar oportunidades em diferentes ambientes de mercado. Seguimos comprometidos com um crescimento disciplinado, pautado pela excelência na execução, pela inovação e por uma gestão rigorosa de riscos. Agradeço aos nossos clientes pela confiança no BTG Pactual e a todos os nossos colaboradores pelo empenho e dedicação, fundamentais para continuarmos gerando valor aos nossos stakeholders”, afirma Roberto Sallouti, CEO do BTG Pactual. BC do Uruguai autoriza BTG a comprar HSBC local O BTG Pactual informou que recebeu autorização do Banco Central do Uruguai (BCU) para a aquisição do HSBC local. A transação, anunciada em julho de 2025, prevê também instrumentos adicionais de capital, por um montante aproximado de US$ 175 milhões. O valor está sujeito a ajustes para refletir os resultados da operação entre 31 de dezembro de 2024 e a data de fechamento do negócio. A operação faz parte da estratégia de crescimento internacional e de ampliação da presença do BTG na América Latina. “Após a conclusão da transação, iniciaremos uma nova etapa de integração da operação local à plataforma global do BTG, ampliando também o acesso de clientes e investidores locais às oportunidades globais da nossa plataforma”, afirma CEO. Atualmente, a instituição possui operações no Brasil, Chile, Colômbia, México, Peru e Argentina. Está presente também na Europa e nos Estados Unidos, onde passou a operar inclusive com licença bancária, após concluir a aquisição do M.Y. Safra Bank em janeiro deste ano. Para o CEO do HSBC Uruguai, Constantino Gotsis, a aprovação do BCU “abre um novo capítulo para o fortalecimento e crescimento do sistema financeiro uruguaio”. Até a conclusão, o banco permanece como parte do Grupo HSBC e seguirá focado em apoiar seus clientes durante a transição. Com informação do Estadão de Conteúdo (Cynthia Decloedt).
